title: Quality of bladder cancer information on YouTube
screen_reason: QUALITY-ONLY study. The paper's stated aim mentions 'the presence of misinformation', but nothing in it judges any video for truth or falsity: the only instruments are DISCERN (16 items, with item 16 dichotomised into poor quality 1-2 vs moderate/good 3-5) and PEMAT understandability/actionability, both reported as scores and as a share of videos below a quality cutoff. There is no external ground truth for accuracy - no fact-check, no guideline-concordance judgement, no false/misleading coding, no source-reliability list - and a wholly accurate video can be scored 'poor quality' for failing to cite sources or state its aims, which is exactly the case the instructions class as QUALITY. Misinformation appears only as an inference in the Conclusions ('This poses a significant risk of misinformation'), not as a measurement. Excluded per the QUALITY-ONLY exclusion in section 1 and the QUALITY-vs-CONTENT rule in section 3; estimates list left empty accordingly.
missed_or_uncertain: Recorded here so nothing is lost if an adjudicator disagrees with the EXCLUDE. All of the paper's shares are quality-instrument shares over the same denominator of 38 Spanish-language bladder-cancer YouTube videos (first 50 results for 'bladder cancer', searched 9 March 2021 in incognito mode, sorted by views, filtered to duration under 4 minutes and excluding videos without text or voice), coded by three urologists: (a) DISCERN poor quality (score 1-2) 26/38 reported as 66.7%; moderate/good (3-5) 12/38 reported as 30.8%; (b) median DISCERN total 34 (range 20-63) and median DISCERN question 16 of 1.5 (1-4.5); (c) median PEMAT understandability 71.6% (16.5-100%) and actionability 35.5% (0-100%) - medians of a scale, with no share of videos above a threshold, so no row would be derivable from these even if the paper were included. Subgroup quality shares: 90.9% of videos starring medical staff were poor quality (20/22) vs 37.5% (6/16) for non-medical speakers (p = 0.01); 94.1% (16/17) of videos without relevant information were poor quality vs 47.5% (10/21) of those with it (p = 0.02); by author 76.5% (13) medical professional vs 61.9% (13) unqualified personnel (p = 0.337); by audience 72.7% (24) general public vs 40% (2) patients (p = 0.301). Descriptive composition shares (audience general public 84.6%; main topic treatment 47.4%; author news media 35.9%; speaker medical personnel 41%; description advertising 13.2%) are content descriptors, not falsity. Figures cited from other papers and excluded per R8 in any case: '77% of prostate cancer videos on YouTube had potentially uninformative content' (Loeb et al. ref 8) and the English-language bladder-cancer comparison (Loeb et al. ref 1: PEMAT 71% and 33%, quality moderate to poor in 67% of videos). ARITHMETIC PROBLEM to flag: the paper states 38 videos analysed and 26 + 12 = 38, but 26/38 = 68.4% and 12/38 = 31.6%, whereas the reported 66.7% and 30.8% correspond to a denominator of 39 (26/39, 12/39) and sum to only 97.5%. The percentages in the abstract, Table 1, Results and Conclusions are therefore all computed on a denominator that does not match the stated sample.

rob.design: Cross-sectional descriptive content analysis. Single YouTube search for 'bladder cancer' in Spanish on 9 March 2021, in incognito mode with no logged-in session; results sorted by number of views, videos shorter than 4 minutes filtered out and videos without text or voice excluded, reducing the first 50 hits to 38 analysed. Each video was assessed by three urologists with two validated instruments (PEMAT, 17 items; DISCERN, 16 items), with DISCERN item 16 dichotomised at 1-2 vs 3-5; univariate comparisons of the poor vs moderate/good groups. No inter-rater reliability statistic, no reconciliation rule between the three raters, and no accuracy or falsity instrument at all. Authors' stated limitations: one platform only, Spanish only, and the under-4-minute filter. Percentage denominators are internally inconsistent (see missed_or_uncertain).
rob.item6_quote: No misinformation case definition exists in the paper; the operative case definition is a quality cutoff: "They were classified according to the latter score into poor quality (1-2 points) and moderate/good quality (3-5 points)."
rob.item10_quote: Thus, 26/38 videos (66.7%) were of poor quality and 12/38 (30.8%) were of moderate or good quality.
